title: Wood Mackenzie forecasts global robotics power demand to reach 363 TWh by 2035, approaching France's entire nuclear output
gist: Wood Mackenzie's 'Embodied AI' research puts global robotics electricity demand at 363 TWh by 2035 — 357 TWh industrial plus 6 TWh humanoid — approaching France's 373 TWh of 2025 nuclear generation, and frames it as a second, largely unmodelled load stacking on top of AI data centre demand. The existing 5 million industrial robots already draw 78 TWh a year, equal to 20-25 percent of global data centre demand, and China controls over 70 percent of industrial robot installations and nearly 90 percent of deployed humanoids.

themes.theme: Robotics as the unmodelled second load

insights.claim: Global robotics electricity consumption is forecast at 363 TWh by 2035 in Wood Mackenzie's base case, approaching France's 373 TWh of nuclear generation in 2025, split between 357 TWh for industrial robots and 6 TWh annually for humanoids.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A France-sized nuclear fleet's worth of new load that most utility capacity plans do not carry — a direct upside surprise risk to 2030s power demand forecasts and to generation/grid capex.
insights.locator: Key findings: Combined global robotics electricity demand

insights.claim: Robotics power demand is a second and largely unmodelled draw on global electricity infrastructure, arriving on top of AI data centre load that is already straining capacity planning.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: If planners are only modelling data centres, the reserve-margin math in developed grids is optimistic — favours long-dated power, transmission and firm-capacity exposure.
insights.quote: making robotics a second and largely unmodelled demand on global electricity infrastructure
insights.locator: The finding arrives as energy capacity planning is already under pressure

insights.claim: Robotics training infrastructure is deliberately excluded from the 363 TWh figure because it is already captured inside data centre demand estimates, meaning the robotics number is incremental to and not overlapping with data centre forecasts.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The two demand curves are additive — analysts stacking robotics onto data centre forecasts are not double-counting, which makes the aggregate load thesis more, not less, aggressive.
insights.quote: Robotics training infrastructure is captured within data centre demand estimates and excluded here to avoid double counting.
insights.locator: Background: Robotics demand has grown for over a decade

insights.claim: Most industrial robots draw power directly from the local grid with no low-carbon sourcing mandates attached, unlike the PPA-driven procurement behaviour of hyperscale data centres.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Robotics load lands on the marginal fossil generator rather than pulling new renewables into the system — bullish for grid-served thermal dispatch and bearish for corporate-PPA-driven renewables demand narratives.
insights.quote: Most industrial robots draw power directly from the local grid, without low-carbon sourcing mandates.
insights.locator: Background: Robotics demand has grown for over a decade

themes.theme: Installed base math and the 12% CAGR assumption

insights.claim: The 5 million industrial robots operating in 2025 already draw 78 TWh a year — almost twice London's electricity consumption and equivalent to 20-25 percent of total global data centre demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Robotics is not a future load — it is already a quarter the size of the data centre load everyone is repricing power markets around.
insights.locator: The 5 million robots in operation today consume 78 TWh a year

insights.claim: The industrial robot fleet is projected to reach 16 million units by 2035, a forecast explicitly conditional on sustaining the current 12 percent annual expansion rate.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The whole 357 TWh industrial number hangs on an unbroken 12 percent CAGR — a single capex recession in manufacturing breaks the load forecast, so track annual installation data as the tell.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie expects the operational fleet to reach 16 million units

insights.claim: Annual industrial robot installations rose from 200,000 in 2015 to 500,000 in 2025 and are forecast to exceed 1 million by 2032, per International Federation of Robotics and Wood Mackenzie data.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A doubling of the annual install rate within seven years sets the volume backdrop for robot OEMs, motion components and factory automation suppliers.

themes.theme: Humanoid cost collapse and unit economics

insights.claim: Average humanoid robot prices fell 93 percent between 2020 and 2025 to US$58,000, with Unitree Robotics' G1 priced at US$16,000 in 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 93 percent price collapse in five years is the classic adoption-curve trigger; the deflation is coming from Chinese suppliers, which compresses margins for Western humanoid entrants.
insights.locator: Increasingly competitive prices are pulling more buyers in

insights.claim: A Unitree G1 running eight hours a day costs an estimated US$82 a year in electricity at a global average industrial tariff of US$0.14 per kWh, far below human labour costs in most markets.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Operating cost is essentially free relative to wages, so the binding constraint on humanoid substitution is capability and power availability, not opex — the labour-displacement case is already economically settled at the margin.
insights.locator: China’s Unitree Robotics' G1 is now priced at US$16,000

insights.claim: Humanoid robot stock is forecast to grow at over 90 percent CAGR from 2025 to 2035, reaching more than 10 million units with annual shipments exceeding 4 million.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 90 percent CAGR implies a supply chain build-out in actuators, batteries and sensors far ahead of current capacity — the bottleneck components are where the returns concentrate.
insights.locator: Humanoid robot stock grows at over 90% CAGR

insights.claim: If the humanoid market reaches one billion units by 2050, humanoid power demand alone could match South Korea's entire 2026 electricity generation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A scenario, not a base case — but it sets the ceiling on how large embodied AI load could become and frames the 6 TWh 2035 humanoid figure as trivially early.
insights.locator: Humanoid robots are still early in rollout but growing fast

themes.theme: China's structural control of the robot supply chain

insights.claim: China accounts for over 70 percent of annual global industrial robot installations and Chinese companies are responsible for nearly 90 percent of all humanoid units deployed in 2025.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Near-monopoly deployment share means embodied AI is a Chinese-supply-chain story by default — Western robotics exposure is a policy and tariff bet as much as a technology bet.
insights.locator: No single country shapes this market more than China

insights.claim: China State Grid has committed US$1 billion in 2026 to procure 8,500 AI-enabled autonomous robots covering more than 600 specialised tasks, from routine grid maintenance to live-line work on ultra-high voltage lines.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: State-owned utilities buying robots at billion-dollar scale signals robotics is being treated as critical national infrastructure in China, implying policy-backed demand that is insensitive to commercial payback periods.
insights.locator: China State Grid illustrates that position directly

themes.theme: Power as the binding constraint on automation

insights.claim: Power availability is becoming a genuine brake on robotic adoption at precisely the moment developed-economy labour markets are running out of alternative sources of workers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frames electricity, not chips or algorithms, as the gating input on the automation response to demographic labour shortage — grid interconnection queues become a macro productivity variable.
insights.quote: Power constraints are becoming a real brake on robotic adoption, and that matters because labour markets in developed economies are running short of alternatives
insights.locator: said Robert Liew, Director, Integrated Energy Research

insights.claim: The decade-long structural drivers of robotics demand are labour shortages, rising labour costs and supply chain security concerns, with AI advances in computer vision, large language models and reinforcement learning extending robots into logistics, healthcare and field operations.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Demand is driven by demographics and reshoring rather than the AI hype cycle, which makes the installation trend more durable through an AI capex pause than data centre spend is.
insights.locator: Background: Robotics demand has grown for over a decade
